samples.text:
In some places, the number of crimes committed by teenagers is increasing and people are worried about this. This essay will discuss why some young people become criminals and what schools should do to prevent it.

There are many reasons why teenagers get involved in crime. One reason is family problems. If parents are divorced or they work all the time, children may not get enough attention and guidance, so they spend time on the streets with bad friends. Peer pressure is also a big reason. Teenagers want to be accepted by their group, so if their friends steal or fight, they do the same things to look cool. In addition, poverty can push young people to commit crime. For example, a teenager from a poor family may steal a phone because he cannot afford to buy one.

In my opinion, schools have a important role in preventing youth crime. Firstly, teachers spend many hours with students every day, so they can notice when a student has problems at home or behave badly. Schools should have counsellors who can talk with these students and helping them. Secondly, schools can offer after-school activities such as sports, music or drama clubs. These activities keep teenagers busy and give them something positive to do, so they have less time for getting in trouble. Finally, schools should teach students about the law and the results of committing a crime.

In conclusion, teenagers commit crimes because of family problems, peer pressure and poverty. Schools cannot solve this problem alone, but they can help a lot by supporting students, organising activities and teaching them about consequences.
samples.why: Both questions addressed with relevant causes and school roles · ideas stated rather than explored · simple sequencing · informal phrasing (look cool) · errors in articles, agreement and verb forms.

samples.text:
Rising levels of teenage crime have become a concern in a number of communities. This essay will consider the main factors that lead some young people into criminal behaviour and argue that schools have an important, though limited, role in preventing it.

A difficult home environment is often at the root of the problem. Teenagers who lack supervision or who experience conflict and neglect at home may look for a sense of belonging elsewhere, sometimes in gangs that offer loyalty and status. Peer influence is closely connected to this. Adolescents are especially sensitive to the approval of their friends, and within certain groups, activities such as shoplifting or vandalism can be seen as a way of proving oneself. Economic disadvantage also plays a part, since young people growing up in deprived areas may have few legitimate opportunities and see crime as an easy way to obtain money or possessions.

Schools are well placed to address several of these factors. Because teachers see students daily, they are often the first adults to notice warning signs such as persistent absence, aggressive behaviour or sudden changes in friendship groups, and they can refer these students to counsellors or social services at an early stage. Schools can also provide constructive alternatives by running after-school clubs, sports teams and mentoring schemes, which give teenagers both supervision and a positive identity. Moreover, keeping students engaged in learning is itself a form of prevention, as those who are excluded or leave early are far more vulnerable to be drawn into crime. However, schools cannot be expected to solve the problem alone, and they need support from families and local authorities.

In conclusion, teenagers become involved in crime mainly because of family difficulties, peer pressure and poverty. Schools can play a valuable role through early intervention, extracurricular activities and keeping students in education, but prevention requires a wider community effort.
samples.why: Clear, qualified position · both questions answered with extended, relevant support · logical organisation with a clear focus per paragraph · good lexical range (deprived areas, warning signs) · one minor grammatical slip.

samples.text:
Teenage crime attracts considerable public attention, and in some areas it appears to be rising. Although there is no single explanation for why young people offend, the most common causes are social rather than individual, and schools, where adolescents spend much of their time, are in a strong position to help prevent it.

The family environment is frequently the starting point. Young people who grow up with little supervision, or amid conflict and instability, may lack both the guidance and the emotional security that discourage risky behaviour. In such circumstances, the pull of peers becomes especially powerful. Adolescence is a stage at which acceptance by one's group matters intensely, and where that group treats theft or violence as a badge of status, the pressure to participate can be difficult to resist. Poverty and a lack of opportunity compound these influences: in neighbourhoods where jobs are scarce and youth facilities have closed, crime may seem to offer money, excitement and respect that are unattainable by legitimate means.

Schools can respond to each of these pressures. With the most regular contact with young people of any institution, they are ideally placed to identify early warning signs, such as truancy, declining grades or abrupt changes in behaviour, and to connect vulnerable students with counselling before problems escalate. They can also offer the sense of belonging that some teenagers seek elsewhere, through sports teams, creative projects and mentoring by trusted adults. Perhaps most importantly, schools should work hard to keep struggling pupils in education rather than resorting quickly to exclusion, since those who drop out are left with time on their hands and diminished prospects. Nevertheless, schools cannot compensate entirely for problems at home, and their efforts are most effective when coordinated with families and local services.

In conclusion, youth crime is driven largely by family instability, peer pressure and lack of opportunity. Schools can make a significant contribution through early identification, positive activities and inclusive policies, but only as part of a broader, coordinated approach.
samples.why: Both questions fully addressed, with causes explicitly matched to school responses · skilful cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary (compound, truancy, escalate) · a wide range of structures used accurately and naturally.
